title: Red spider mites in cabbage - Tanzania

Header: Red spider mites in cabbage - Tanzania
Tetranychus spp. Utitiri mwekundu in Swahili

Prevention: Place nursery away from infested cabbage or tomato fields.
Avoid transplanting next to infested fields.
Remove mite-hosting weeds or volunteer tomatoes.
Furrow irrigate or flood irrigate regularly to remove dust with mites (2-3 x per week in dry season).
Note that moist conditions can promote certain diseases.
Tagetes (Marigold), lemongrass, garlic, or legumes such as
Crotolaria (Marejea) around field to repel mites.
Avoid chemicals, as they can kill rove beetles ( Oligota ) that eat mites.
Remove and bury or burn all infested crop residues immediately after harvest as many mites live in there.
Rotate cabbage with 2 seasons of non- brassica crops, e.g.
Do not rotate with tomatoes because they harbour mites.
Monitoring: Spider mites can be a problem in dry weather.
Scout for damage once/twice per week, from transplanting to head formation.
Scout for tiny whitish spots of mite feeding on both sides of the leaves:
If 3-8 out of 20 plants have plenty of spots, consider action.
Look on both sides of the leaves for mite webbing: consider action when 1 leaf per plant on average has webbing.
Direct Control: Always spray in mornings reaching coverage of upper and lower surface of leaves of younger plants.
Spray max twice in two weeks interval:
Red hot chilli pepper soap solution, neem seed or leaf extract-soap mixture, or cotton-seed-oil soap mixture.
Finely apply ash dust over moist cabbage plants in nurseries.
Smear small wooden sticks with cooking oil; place them between cabbage rows to attract ants that eat mites.
Strong water sprays and sprinkler irrigation drop mites to the ground, but can enhance cabbage diseases.
Restrictions: Only use pesticides that kill mites.
Search for the word acaricide (= mite pesticide) on the product label.
When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label.
